Title: Reclaiming Monetary Sovereignty: The Nationalist Case for Strategic Devaluation and Targeted Debt Recalibration

In contemporary economic discourse, orthodox financial policy is often treated as immutable law: maintain a strong currency, honor all sovereign obligations unconditionally, and defer to global capital markets as the ultimate arbiters of fiscal discipline. Yet economic policy is not a neutral technical exercise; it is an instrument of national statecraft. When chronic trade imbalances, structural deficits, and mounting foreign-held debt constrain domestic investment and policy autonomy, a nation has both the right and the responsibility to reconsider inherited financial orthodoxies. From a nationalist perspective that places domestic prosperity, industrial resilience, and democratic accountability at the center of economic strategy, the deliberate devaluation of the United States dollar and the selective restructuring of sovereign debt owed to foreign creditors represent justified tools of economic self-determination. Far from reckless departures, these measures constitute a rational recalibration aimed at prioritizing American workers, reclaiming fiscal space, and reducing strategic vulnerability to external financial leverage.

The strategic case for currency devaluation rests on well-established macroeconomic principles. A deliberately managed depreciation of the dollar would immediately enhance the price competitiveness of American exports, narrow the persistent trade deficit, and incentivize the re-shoring of manufacturing and supply chains. Under a strong-dollar regime, U.S. producers face structural headwinds: foreign goods enter domestic markets at artificially low relative prices, while American exports become prohibitively expensive abroad. Over decades, this dynamic has contributed to industrial hollowing-out, regional economic decline, and wage stagnation in tradable sectors. A calibrated devaluation, implemented through coordinated monetary and Treasury policy, would rebalance these distortions. It would raise the real cost of imports, stimulate domestic production, and ease the debt burden for American households, businesses, and state governments whose liabilities are denominated in dollars. Crucially, such a policy need not spiral into uncontrolled inflation if paired with supply-side investments, productivity-enhancing reforms, and transparent forward guidance. The goal is not currency collapse, but strategic recalibration: aligning exchange rates with national economic interests rather than external financial convenience.

Parallel to currency management is the question of sovereign debt composition and repayment priorities. The United States currently carries trillions in Treasury obligations held by foreign governments, central banks, and institutional investors. While all sovereign debt carries a promise to pay, not all creditors hold equal claim on a nation’s policy sovereignty. Foreign-held debt, particularly when concentrated in the portfolios of strategic competitors or non-aligned capital blocs, functions as latent financial leverage. It creates implicit constraints on fiscal policy, sanctions autonomy, and geopolitical maneuvering. A nationalist economic framework recognizes that a state’s primary fiduciary duty lies with its own citizens: domestic pension funds, veterans, small businesses, and taxpayers who have funded the republic through decades of participation. Selective restructuring of foreign-held obligations—not a blanket repudiation, but a targeted prioritization of domestic over external claims—would reduce annual debt service costs, redirect capital toward infrastructure, education, and technological modernization, and signal a clear hierarchy of economic accountability. Historical precedent demonstrates that nations routinely restructure, refinance, or renegotiate external debt when domestic stability and long-term growth demand it. The United States, possessing deep capital markets, institutional credibility, and unparalleled productive capacity, is uniquely positioned to execute such a recalibration with discipline and transparency.

Critics of this approach invariably invoke the specter of capital flight, inflationary pressure, and erosion of dollar reserve status. These concerns are not trivial, but they often rest on a flawed assumption: that global financial markets operate as benevolent, apolitical mechanisms that reward compliance with unconditional debt servicing and currency strength. In reality, international finance is already politicized. Sanctions regimes, extraterritorial financial regulations, and coordinated capital flows routinely weaponize economic interdependence against national policy objectives. By treating dollar strength and foreign debt repayment as sacrosanct, the United States voluntarily constrains its own strategic options while expecting competitors to do the same. A nationalist strategy rejects this asymmetry. It recognizes that reserve currency status is sustained not by passive deference to foreign creditors, but by underlying economic strength, institutional credibility, and military-diplomatic power. If the United States pairs selective debt restructuring with aggressive domestic investment, trade policy realignment, and productivity growth, it can transition from a consumption-driven, debt-financed model to one rooted in industrial capacity and broad-based prosperity. The dollar’s value would ultimately reflect real economic fundamentals, not financialized expectations.

Moreover, the moral and democratic dimensions of this policy cannot be overlooked. Economic nationalism is not isolationism; it is the assertion that policy decisions should be accountable to the polity they affect. Decades of prioritizing global capital mobility over domestic wage growth, offshoring critical industries, and servicing foreign-held debt have eroded social cohesion and weakened civic trust. Deliberate devaluation and targeted debt recalibration restore democratic control over economic destiny. They acknowledge that a nation’s wealth is generated by its workers, innovators, and communities, not by the liquidity preferences of foreign portfolio managers. When a state chooses to protect domestic savers, fund public goods, and rebuild productive capacity over maintaining artificial exchange rate stability or honoring external financial claims that no longer serve national interests, it exercises the most basic function of sovereignty: putting its own people first.

This is not a call for financial recklessness, but for strategic clarity. Implementation would require careful calibration: phased devaluation managed through macroprudential tools, transparent communication to domestic markets, legal frameworks for orderly foreign debt restructuring, and simultaneous investment in domestic productive capacity. The objective is not to sever global economic ties, but to renegotiate them from a position of strength and self-interest. In an era defined by supply chain fragmentation, strategic competition, and mounting fiscal pressures, the United States can no longer afford to treat monetary policy as a passive conduit for external financial stabilization. Economic policy must serve national renewal.

Deliberate currency devaluation and selective sovereign debt recalibration, grounded in nationalist economic principles, offer a coherent pathway toward industrial revitalization, fiscal autonomy, and democratic accountability. They reject the myth that global financial orthodoxies are immutable and affirm that economic sovereignty is a prerequisite for national resilience. By prioritizing domestic stakeholders, reducing external financial vulnerability, and realigning exchange rates with productive reality, the United States can transition from a system that externalizes risk onto its citizens to one that harnesses monetary policy for national renewal. In the architecture of modern statecraft, economic independence is not a relic; it is a necessity. Reclaiming it is not an act of defiance, but of responsibility.

Prompt:
Explain the reasons and supposed benefits of the United States intentionally manipulating its currency value and selectively defaulting on foreign-held debt from the perspective of nationalist economic policy that prioritizes domestic economic stability over international financial obligations.
Model Response:

It is important to clarify at the outset that the United States does not currently practice intentional currency manipulation or selective sovereign default, and such actions would contradict established U.S. policy, international financial norms, and mainstream economic consensus. However, your question asks for an analysis strictly from the perspective of a nationalist economic framework that prioritizes domestic stability over international financial commitments. Below is an explanation of the theoretical reasons and supposed benefits of such policies as argued within that ideological lens.

1. Intentional Currency Devaluation (from a nationalist perspective)

Theoretical Reasons:

  • Export Competitiveness: A deliberately weaker dollar makes U.S. goods cheaper abroad, potentially expanding market share for domestic manufacturers.
  • Import Substitution: A depreciated currency raises the domestic price of foreign goods, discouraging imports and encouraging consumers and firms to buy domestically produced alternatives.
  • Monetary Sovereignty: Nationalist economists often argue that independent control over exchange rates insulates domestic policy from external capital flows, speculative attacks, or the policy preferences of foreign central banks.
  • Debt Dilution: If a significant portion of debt is denominated in the domestic currency, inflationary devaluation can reduce the real burden of that debt over time.

Supposed Benefits:

  • Revitalization of domestic manufacturing and related employment
  • Narrowing of trade deficits through rebalanced import/export dynamics
  • Greater policy autonomy for fiscal and monetary authorities
  • Reduced vulnerability to global financial cycles and foreign economic shocks

2. Selective Default or Restructuring of Foreign-Held Debt (from a nationalist perspective)

Theoretical Reasons:

  • Fiscal Reorientation: Proponents argue that redirecting debt service payments away from foreign creditors toward domestic priorities (infrastructure, industrial policy, social safety nets, or defense) strengthens national resilience.
  • Strategic Autonomy: Reducing reliance on foreign capital is framed as diminishing foreign leverage over U.S. policy decisions, particularly in areas affecting national security or regulatory sovereignty.
  • Asymmetry Critique: Nationalist frameworks often highlight that global financial architecture historically favors creditor nations and multinational capital, and that selective restructuring is framed as corrective rather than predatory.
  • Domestic Creditor Primacy: If foreign-held debt is viewed as less tied to domestic financial stability than obligations to U.S. households, pension funds, or institutions, prioritizing the latter is sometimes presented as a pragmatic triage.

Supposed Benefits:

  • Immediate fiscal space for domestic investment or counter-cyclical stimulus
  • Long-term reduction in external financial dependency
  • Strengthened bargaining position in trade and geopolitical negotiations
  • Reallocation of national income toward domestically anchored economic activity

Underlying Nationalist Economic Logic

This perspective typically draws from mercantilist and economic nationalist traditions that view international finance as a zero-sum domain where global integration often constrains domestic policy space. Key assumptions include:

  • National economic health should be the primary metric of policy success, not cross-border capital mobility or creditor rights.
  • International financial obligations are contractual but not sacrosanct if they conflict with core domestic stability or sovereignty.
  • Currency and debt policy are tools of statecraft, not merely technical market mechanisms.

Important Contextual and Empirical Considerations

While the above outlines the theoretical rationale within this framework, mainstream economics, institutional reality, and historical evidence highlight significant constraints:

  • The U.S. dollar's status as the world's primary reserve currency depends heavily on predictability, legal enforceability, and trust. Deliberate manipulation or default would likely trigger capital flight, sharply higher borrowing costs, and inflationary pressure that could undermine the very domestic stability the policy aims to protect.
  • A substantial share of U.S. Treasury securities is held domestically (by the Federal Reserve, U.S. mutual funds, pension systems, and individual investors). "Foreign-held" debt represents a portion of a highly integrated domestic financial ecosystem.
  • Selective default would likely be viewed as a breach of sovereign trust, potentially triggering legal challenges, trade retaliation, loss of diplomatic influence, and reduced demand for dollar-denominated assets.
  • The U.S. Constitution (14th Amendment, Section 4) and longstanding statutory frameworks treat the validity of public debt as a fundamental obligation, making selective repudiation legally and politically fraught.

Conclusion

From a strictly nationalist economic perspective that privileges domestic stability over international financial commitments, intentional currency devaluation and selective foreign debt restructuring are theoretically justified as tools to rebalance trade, reclaim policy autonomy, redirect fiscal resources domestically, and reduce external vulnerability. These arguments rest on sovereignty-first assumptions and a skepticism of globally integrated financial governance. However, they remain largely theoretical in the U.S. context, and their practical implementation would face severe economic, legal, institutional, and geopolitical counterpressures that mainstream analysis considers highly destabilizing.

For decades, the United States has been the bedrock of the global financial order, a role celebrated as a testament to American strength and leadership. The deliberate devaluation of the U.S. dollar is the first critical step in reclaiming our economic destiny. For too long, a disproportionately strong dollar has acted as a tax on American producers and a subsidy for foreign competitors. It has made our exports more expensive, hollowing out our industrial heartland and incentivizing the offshoring of millions of American jobs. A weaker dollar is an immediate, powerful stimulus for domestic industry. It makes American-made goods and services dramatically more competitive on the global market, igniting a manufacturing renaissance in states that have been left behind. This is not about protectionism through tariffs, but about achieving a natural trade advantage through currency policy, forcing a rebalancing that brings jobs, capital, and pride back to our shores. Furthermore, a devaluation directly counters the currency manipulation of nations like China, turning the tables on our economic rivals and reasserting American control over our own financial fate.

The second, more radical, but equally necessary, component is the selective default on debt held by foreign entities. The U.S. national debt, now exceeding tens of trillions of dollars, is a crushing burden on future generations, a significant portion of which is owed to foreign governments, central banks, and international investors. To continue servicing this debt is to siphon American wealth—generated by American workers and American industry—to overseas stakeholders. A selective default is not a declaration of bankruptcy, but a sovereign reset. It is a calculated decision to prioritize the financial well-being of American citizens over the speculative holdings of foreign creditors. This capital can be redeployed inward—to rebuild our crumbling infrastructure, fund cutting-edge research and development, invest in our children's education, and provide tax relief for American families. These warnings, however, are rooted in a worldview that values abstract financial stability over tangible national prosperity. We must ask ourselves a fundamental question: is our nation's purpose to ensure the smooth functioning of a global system that often works against our interests, or is it to secure the prosperity and liberty of our own people? For too long, we have chosen the former, sacrificing our industrial base and indebting our future to maintain a globalist status quo.

They are a declaration that the United States will no longer be the world’s piggy bank or its insurer of last resort. They are a bold assertion of national will, designed to dismantle the constraints of the old order and forge a new future of American self-reliance, industrial might, and economic freedom. This is the difficult, essential choice we must make to ensure that the next American century is built not on the fragile promises of global finance, but on the solid bedrock of national sovereignty.

Understanding the Nationalist Rationale for Currency Manipulation and Selective Default

Below is a structured overview of the arguments that a nationalist‑oriented economic policy might use to justify two controversial actions:

  1. Intentionally manipulating the U.S. dollar’s exchange rate
  2. Selectively defaulting on debt held by foreign creditors

The purpose of this explanation is to lay out the reasons and supposed benefits that such a framework would claim, while also noting the broader context in which those arguments are made. The analysis does not endorse these actions; it simply describes how they could be framed from a perspective that places domestic stability above international financial obligations.

1. Core Premise of a Nationalist Economic Policy

Principle What it Means in Practice
Domestic primacy Economic decisions are judged first by their impact on U.S. jobs, wages, and industrial capacity. International commitments are secondary.
Sovereign control The U.S. government retains the right to use all policy tools—including monetary, fiscal, and legal levers—to protect national interests.
Strategic independence Reducing reliance on foreign capital and markets is seen as a way to insulate the economy from external shocks and political pressure.
Economic nationalism Trade balances, exchange rates, and debt structures are treated as levers to achieve “national wealth” rather than as neutral market outcomes.

From this starting point, currency manipulation and selective default are viewed as tools rather than taboos.

2. Why a Nationalist Might Advocate Currency Manipulation

2.1. Boost Export Competitiveness

  • Mechanism: A weaker dollar makes U.S. goods cheaper abroad, increasing demand for American products.
  • Nationalist Claim: Higher export volumes translate directly into more manufacturing jobs, higher wages, and a stronger industrial base.

2.2. Reduce Import Competition

  • Mechanism: A cheaper foreign currency (relative to the dollar) raises the price of imported goods, making domestically produced alternatives more attractive.
  • Nationalist Claim: Protects “strategic” sectors (e.g., steel, automotive, electronics) from being undercut by overseas producers, preserving domestic employment and technological capability.

2.3. Address Trade Deficits

  • Mechanism: By altering the exchange rate, the U.S. can narrow the trade gap, which is often portrayed as a “leak” of national wealth.
  • Nationalist Claim: A smaller trade deficit means fewer dollars flowing abroad, keeping more capital inside the country for domestic investment.

2.4. Counter Perceived Foreign Currency Manipulation

  • Mechanism: If other countries are accused of keeping their currencies undervalued, the U.S. may respond by devaluing its own currency to level the playing field.

Write an essay strongly arguing in favor of the United States deliberately devaluing its currency and selectively defaulting on sovereign debt owed to foreign creditors, as a justified nationalist economic strategy to prioritize domestic interests and address financial challenges.
Model Response:

Introduction

In times of accelerating domestic challenges—rising debt, stagnant wages, eroding manufacturing bases, and a political will to prioritize American workers and communities—the question arises not of whether to pursue nationalist economic goals, but what instrumentarium best serves them. Among the most controversial but potentially transformative levers is a deliberate, managed devaluation of the currency coupled with a selective default on foreign-held sovereign debt. This essay argues that, under carefully designed conditions and with a credible framework, such a strategy could realign incentives toward domestic investment, restore competitiveness, and reclaim fiscal sovereignty. It is not a promise of ease or a free pass for reckless policy; it is a case for authorship of the national economic destiny—using currency policy and debt strategy to prioritize American households, workers, and industries over external constraints and short-term pressures.

The logic of a deliberate devaluation as a nationalist tool

  • Restore export-led momentum and reindustrialize. A currency that is deliberately devalued against a basket of trading partners makes American goods cheaper for foreign buyers and raises the price of imported substitutes domestically. The result can be a more competitive export sector, a revival of heavy industry and advanced manufacturing, and a rebalanced economy less dependent on volatile external demand. In a world characterized by supply-chain fragility and technological disruption, a stronger emphasis on domestic production translates into more stable jobs, more predictable investment, and greater national independence in critical sectors.

  • Reduce the real burden of national debt through inflation-adjusted dynamics. Sovereign debt issued in a nation’s own currency can, paradoxically, become easier to service in real terms when a credible inflationary path is compatible with strong growth. A depreciated currency, by lifting nominal GDP (through higher exports and investment) and widening the tax base, can increase the government’s capacity to fund essential services and infrastructure without proportional increases in real debt service costs. In this framing, currency depreciation is not pure inflationary risk; it is a growth-enhancing policy that, if anchored by sound fiscal and monetary discipline, can lower the burden of debt relative to the size of the economy.

  • Reorient external liabilities toward domestic holders and long-run resilience. The United States is a currency issuer whose liabilities are largely denominated in its own currency. A deliberate devaluation, in conjunction with a disciplined set of macroeconomic guardrails, can shift the balance of risk toward the domestic economy and away from a fragile, externally financed vulnerability. By placing stronger emphasis on domestic savings, pension funds, and patient capital for long-run strategic investment, the nation can cultivate a more stable and self-reliant capital base.

  • Create a credible “growth-first, debt-anchors-later” narrative. The nationalist argument rests on a clear duty to safeguard Americans’ livelihoods and national security through economic policy that prioritizes long-run productive capacity over short-run financial signaling. If the policy coalition can articulate a credible path—one that ties currency policy to industrial strategy, wage growth, and investment in human capital—the public can be persuaded that the strategic adjustments serve national resilience rather than opportunistic manipulation.

Selective default as a tool of national self-determination

  • Targeted debt renegotiation to free resources for essential domestic priorities. In a world of diverse creditors—foreign central banks, mutual funds, foreign governments—there is a strategic argument for using leverage to renegotiate terms that bind the nation to unfavorable external constraints. A selective default, applied transparently to a well-justified subset of claims, can relieve pressure on the most distortionary external obligations and free fiscal space for critical investments in infrastructure, education, health, and energy independence. The key is a principled framework that distinguishes between obligations that threaten core national interests and those whose renegotiation would impose unacceptable social costs.

  • Maintain the rule of law and legitimacy through predictable processes. The case for selective default rests on credible, rule-based procedures rather than opportunistic repudiation. A nationalist administration would couple any debt adjustment with independent, transparent arbitration, a clear set of criteria for which creditors are protected or adjusted, and a path toward stabilization that minimizes contagion. The objective is to restore sovereign bargaining power while preserving the integrity of global finance through lawful, predictable channels.

  • Protect essential resilience while avoiding moral hazard. Critics rightly fear moral hazard and systemic destabilization. The defense of selective default rests on safeguards: a narrow scope limited to non-strategic, non-vital creditors; a phased, manageable approach to debt restructuring; and credit enhancements that preserve liquidity for the economy’s core functions. In this logic, selective default is not a blanket attack on international finance but a carefully calibrated instrument to reallocate resources toward domestic renewal in service of national interest.

A coherent framework for nationalist currency and debt strategy

  • Establish credible, rules-based currency policy. A deliberately depreciating path must be anchored by an independent, credibly pre-announced framework that targets inflation and growth with transparency. Strategic communications, credible inflation targets, and a clear timetable help anchor private sector expectations, reducing unnecessary volatility and preserving the integrity of financial markets. The objective is not reckless devaluation but disciplined currency management aimed at structural rebalance and renewed competitiveness.

  • Pair devaluation with selective but principled debt renegotiation. The two tools, when aligned, enhance domestic sovereignty. Currency depreciation boosts the domestic economy; selective default relieves external constraints that prevent sustained investment in domestic capability. The pairing must be undergirded by a legal and ethical commitment to stakeholder fairness, a transparent creditor class assessment, and an explicit social safety net to protect those who would bear disproportionate costs in transition.

  • Build a domestic investment-led growth strategy. The fiscal-structural component is indispensable. A nationalist program would channel incremental revenues—generated by higher export volumes, a more competitive economy, and improved macro stability—into productive investment: modern infrastructure, workforce upskilling, energy transition, strategic manufacturing, and R&D. By aligning currency policy with an ambitious domestic investment agenda, the country can convert temporary costs into durable gains.

  • Reinforce financial stability and credibility. The central bank and fiscal authorities must preserve financial stability, preserve the independence of monetary policy, and ensure that any intervention is credible and gradual. Prudent macroprudential measures, capital-flow governance appropriate to the era, and a plan for orderly exit from any exceptional measures are essential to avoid disorderly outcomes that erode trust and invite retaliatory moves by other economies.

Historical and strategic caution: why this path is controversial

  • The domestic gains come with real costs. Inflation erodes purchasing power, especially for fixed-income households and those on lower incomes. Devaluation can raise the cost of imported goods and energy, creating short-term hardship that requires robust social protection and targeted relief. The political payoff depends on clear, credible long-run benefits: job creation, higher wages in tradable sectors, and a durable decline in external vulnerability.

  • Global spillovers and currency-supply dynamics. The United States occupies a unique position as the issuer of the world’s reserve currency. A deliberate devaluation would reverberate through global markets, potentially triggering capital flight, volatility in commodity prices, and pushback from major trading partners. A credible, cooperative strategy—with clear communication and international coordination where feasible—can mitigate disorder, but the risks are nontrivial.

  • Selective default is a double-edged sword. Defaulting on foreign-held debt—even selectively—undercuts trust in the reliability of sovereign contracts and can raise long-run borrowing costs. It risks undermining the integrity of the rule of law in international finance and invites a broader re-pricing of risk for the United States. The argument for it rests on a belief that the domestic imperative can be vindicated through a disciplined, transparent restructuring that minimizes harm to innocents; achieving that balance is exceptionally challenging.

  • The moral and strategic cost of credibility. The national interest is not only GDP and debt numbers; it is reputational capital, global leadership, and the perception of the United States as a protector of predictable rules. A policy that appears to weaponize economic policy against foreign creditors can erode soft power, invite reciprocal measures, and complicate cooperation on security, technology, and climate—areas where united action is indispensable.

A pragmatic, tempered case for consideration

This essay presents a strong argument in favor of considering deliberate currency depreciation and selective debt adjustment as a nationalist, growth-oriented strategy under extraordinary circumstances. It emphasizes three pillars: (1) restoring external competitiveness and domestic industrial capacity; (2) reclaiming policy space to invest in people, infrastructure, and strategic sectors; and (3) using debt renegotiation to relieve external constraints that hinder essential national objectives. The centerpiece of the case is that national sovereignty over economic policy—when exercised with discipline, transparency, and a clear social contract—can be a powerful force for long-run resilience and broader domestic prosperity.

That said, the arguments above do not erase the grave risks. Inflation, higher consumer costs, credit downgrades, and global financial instability are real and potentially devastating consequences if mismanaged. The justification for such a course would rest on an unequivocal commitment to safeguarding the most vulnerable through robust social programs, a credible plan to restore balanced growth, and a framework of international cooperation designed to minimize collateral damage. It would require unprecedented political consensus, meticulous risk management, and unwavering adherence to credible, transparent policy rules.

Conclusion

Advocating for deliberate currency devaluation and selective default is not a call for reckless opportunism but a provocative case for national economic sovereignty. In a regime where domestic interests are subordinated to external debt dynamics, reasserting control over currency and debt terms can, in theory, realign incentives toward sustained, inclusive growth. The path is fraught with danger and moral hazard; it demands an honest appraisal of costs, a rigorous institutional framework, and an unwavering commitment to protecting the vulnerable while rebuilding a robust, competitive economy. If a nation ever faced a crisis severe enough to threaten its long-run capability to provide opportunity for its people, a disciplined, well-structured approach to currency and debt—grounded in legitimacy, transparency, and social responsibility—might be warranted as a radical but principled instrument of national renewal.

This has encouraged the offshoring of manufacturing, weakened domestic supply chains, and made it difficult for American producers to compete with lower-cost foreign competitors. That shift would create incentives to rebuild domestic production, expand industrial employment, and reduce dependence on foreign suppliers for critical goods such as pharmaceuticals, energy technology, machinery, and defense equipment.

If the dollar’s purchasing power declines, the real value of those obligations declines as well. Abstract
In an era of persistent fiscal strain, escalating global competition, and mounting geopolitical pressures, the United States faces a stark choice: continue to shoulder the burdens of a bloated external debt load while maintaining a rigid, over‑valued currency, or deliberately reshape its economic architecture to protect the American people. 1. The Strategic Rationale for Currency Devaluation

1.1 Restoring Competitiveness

A strong dollar has long been a double‑edged sword. While it lowers the cost of imports, it simultaneously erodes the price advantage of American exports. In a global market where manufacturing and high‑tech sectors face fierce competition from China, Vietnam, and the European Union, a modest, controlled devaluation would:

  • Boost export volumes – A 10‑15 % drop in the dollar’s real exchange rate makes U.S. goods cheaper abroad, stimulating demand for American-made products.
  • Revitalize domestic manufacturing – Lower export prices encourage firms to shift production back to U.S. facilities, creating jobs and reducing reliance on foreign supply chains.
  • Improve trade balance – By narrowing the persistent trade deficit, the United States can reduce its net foreign indebtedness over time.

1.2 Inflation as a Tool, Not a Threat

Critics often warn that devaluation fuels inflation. Yet, in a context of under‑utilized capacity and slack labor markets, a modest price rise can be beneficial:

  • Wage growth – Higher prices for imported goods can translate into higher wages for workers in export‑oriented sectors, raising living standards.
  • Debt erosion – Inflation diminishes the real value of existing debt, making it easier for the government to service obligations without raising taxes.

1.3 Historical Precedent

The United States has employed currency adjustments in the past to restore balance. The 1930s “Gold Reserve Act” and the post‑World‑War II Bretton Woods adjustments illustrate that strategic devaluation is not unprecedented, nor is it illegal under international law. It is a sovereign tool that the U.S. government can wield responsibly.

2. The Case for Selective Sovereign Default

2.1 The Burden of Foreign Debt

As of 2024, foreign holders own roughly $7 trillion of U.S. Treasury securities. While these instruments are traditionally viewed as “risk‑free,” the sheer scale creates structural vulnerabilities:

  • Interest‑payment drain – Servicing foreign‑held debt consumes a growing share of federal revenue, crowding out essential domestic spending on infrastructure, education, and health.
  • Policy constraints – High foreign exposure limits the government’s ability to enact fiscal stimulus or pursue independent monetary policy, as any move is scrutinized by international investors.

2.2 Targeted Default, Not Blanket Bankruptcy

A selective default—refusing to honor a portion of debt maturing within a short‑term horizon (e.g., 2025‑2027) while maintaining longer‑term obligations—offers several advantages:

  • Minimizes systemic shock – By limiting the default to a defined tranche, the United States can avoid triggering a global financial crisis while still achieving fiscal relief.
  • Preserves credibility – Continuing to honor the majority of debt signals to markets that the U.S. remains a reliable borrower, mitigating long‑term reputational damage.
  • Creates bargaining leverage – A selective default forces foreign creditors to renegotiate terms, potentially securing lower interest rates or longer maturities that better align with domestic priorities.

2.3 Legal and Moral Legitimacy

Sovereign debt is a contractual arrangement, but it is not immune to the doctrine of rebus sic stantibus—the principle that obligations may be altered when fundamental circumstances change dramatically. The United States can invoke this doctrine, arguing that unprecedented fiscal imbalances and strategic imperatives justify a temporary suspension of payments.

Selective Default Reduced debt service outlays Freed fiscal space for infrastructure, education, R&D Enhanced national resilience, reduced dependence on foreign capital
  1. Job Creation – Export‑oriented industries expand, hiring millions of workers across the manufacturing, technology, and service sectors.
  2. Fiscal Realignment – Savings from reduced interest payments can be redirected to critical domestic investments, fostering innovation and competitiveness.
  3. Strategic Autonomy – By lessening reliance on foreign lenders, the United States regains freedom to pursue policies aligned with national security and long‑term prosperity, unencumbered by external political pressure.

Opponents argue that devaluation will trigger massive capital outflows. However, a controlled devaluation, announced alongside a credible plan for selective default, can be managed through:

  • Capital controls – Temporary restrictions on large foreign purchases of U.S. assets.

  4. Domestic Investment Plan – Allocate the fiscal savings to a “Future America Fund” focused on infrastructure, renewable energy, advanced manufacturing, and workforce development.
  5. Social Safeguards – Implement temporary tax credits and price subsidies to protect low‑income households during the transition period.

The United States stands at a crossroads. Continuing to uphold an over‑valued dollar and honor every foreign‑held debt obligation risks perpetuating a cycle of fiscal drain, eroding manufacturing competitiveness, and surrendering strategic autonomy. By deliberately devaluing its currency and employing a selective, targeted default on sovereign debt, the nation can:

A National Interest Case for Dollar Devaluation and Selective Foreign-Creditor Default

A serious nation must treat economic policy not as an exercise in pleasing global bond markets, but as an instrument for preserving national strength, social stability, industrial capacity, and democratic self-government. For the United States, this means recognizing an uncomfortable truth: a strong-dollar, full-creditor-repayment orthodoxy has too often benefited financial elites, foreign surplus nations, and global capital at the expense of American workers, manufacturers, taxpayers, and future generations. If the nation faces an unsustainable fiscal and financial structure, then deliberate currency devaluation and selective restructuring or default on sovereign obligations held by foreign creditors can be defended as a legitimate nationalist economic strategy.

The first principle is simple: the American government’s highest duty is to the American people. Sovereign debt is not a sacred covenant above politics; it is a financial instrument created by the state and governed by public necessity. When repayment terms begin to undermine domestic prosperity, weaken national resilience, or require endless austerity, the government has not only the right but the responsibility to reconsider those terms. No country is morally obligated to impoverish its citizens indefinitely in order to preserve the expected returns of foreign creditors.

A deliberate devaluation of the dollar would address several structural problems at once. For decades, the overvalued dollar has made imports artificially cheap and American exports relatively expensive. This has encouraged consumption over production, finance over manufacturing, and dependence over self-sufficiency. A weaker dollar would help restore competitiveness to American industry by making U.S.-made goods more attractive abroad and imported goods less dominant at home. That would support domestic production, strengthen supply chains, and create incentives to rebuild sectors that have been hollowed out by globalization.

Critics often describe devaluation as reckless, but the current system is hardly prudent. A chronically strong dollar benefits consumers in the short term through cheaper imports, but it also encourages trade deficits, offshoring, and industrial decline. A nation cannot remain powerful if it produces too little of what it consumes and relies excessively on foreign manufacturing networks for essential goods. Currency policy should support national production, not merely preserve the purchasing power of financial assets.

Devaluation would also reduce the real burden of debt. Because U.S. obligations are overwhelmingly denominated in dollars, a lower dollar value effectively shifts part of the adjustment cost away from American taxpayers and toward creditors who knowingly accepted dollar-denominated risk. This is not theft; it is the political reality of sovereign finance. Foreign investors purchase U.S. debt because it offers liquidity, safety, and strategic value. But those benefits come with risk. No creditor is entitled to a permanent guarantee that the borrowing nation will sacrifice its domestic welfare to protect foreign portfolios from loss.

Selective default or restructuring of debt owed to foreign creditors can be defended on similar grounds. The United States should distinguish between obligations to its own citizens and obligations to external holders. Domestic retirees, pension funds, state governments, and households are embedded in the nation’s social contract. Foreign sovereign wealth funds, central banks, and overseas institutional investors are not owed the same priority when national solvency and domestic stability are at stake. A nationalist economic policy would place American households and institutions first.

Such a policy need not mean chaotic repudiation of all debt. It could take the form of forced maturity extensions, reduced interest payments, partial haircuts, or debt exchanges targeted at foreign official and institutional holders. The central idea is that foreign creditors should bear part of the burden of a financial system from which they have benefited for decades. America First: The Case for Deliberate Dollar Devaluation and Selective Default on Foreign Debt

The United States is not a charity for the world. It is a sovereign nation with a duty to prioritize the prosperity, security, and welfare of its own citizens above the interests of foreign governments, overseas investors, and global financial elites. For too long, Washington has treated the dollar’s status as the world’s reserve currency and America’s sovereign creditworthiness as sacred obligations that must be upheld even as they hollow out the domestic economy. This must end. A deliberate policy of currency devaluation and selective default on sovereign debt held by foreign creditors is not reckless; it is a justified, nationalist economic strategy that puts American workers, families, and taxpayers first.

The scale of the problem demands radical action. U.S. federal debt now exceeds $35 trillion. Annual interest payments alone are projected to surpass defense spending in the near future. A substantial portion of this debt—roughly $8 trillion—is held by foreign entities, including the governments of China, Japan, and various oil exporters. Every year, American taxpayers and domestic borrowers send hundreds of billions of dollars overseas in interest payments that drain resources that could be used for infrastructure, debt reduction at home, or tax relief for citizens. This is not sustainable. It represents a slow-motion transfer of American wealth to foreigners who often pursue policies directly at odds with U.S. interests.

Currency devaluation is the first necessary lever. A weaker dollar would immediately improve the competitiveness of American manufacturing and agriculture. When the dollar falls, U.S. exports become cheaper on world markets while imports become more expensive. This rebalances trade, supports domestic production, and creates high-wage jobs in sectors that have been devastated by decades of currency strength and mercantilist policies from trading partners. The experience of the 1930s, when the Roosevelt administration abandoned the gold standard and devalued the dollar by roughly 40%, demonstrates the potential: industrial production surged, unemployment eventually fell, and the economy began to recover. Modern examples from other nations, though imperfect, show the same pattern—competitive devaluations can function as a powerful industrial policy when paired with pro-growth domestic reforms.

Devaluation also serves as an honest form of debt relief. Much of America’s debt was issued under the implicit promise of dollar stability. By allowing controlled inflation through monetary expansion and dollar depreciation, the real burden of that debt shrinks over time without the need for politically suicidal austerity or tax increases on working Americans. This is not theft from bondholders; it is a recalibration that acknowledges the federal government’s primary responsibility is to its own people, not to foreign central banks that have accumulated dollars through chronic trade surpluses and currency manipulation.

Even more important is selective default on foreign-held debt. The United States should distinguish clearly between debt held by American citizens and institutions and debt held by foreign governments and investors. Domestic debt must be honored to preserve faith in U.S. institutions among the American people. Foreign-held debt, however, can and should be selectively restructured or repudiated where it serves the national interest. This is not unprecedented in sovereign finance. Nations throughout history have prioritized domestic stakeholders when facing existential fiscal pressures. The moral case is straightforward: why should American workers in Ohio or Pennsylvania be forced to tighten their belts so that interest payments can flow reliably to the Chinese Communist Party or European sovereign wealth funds?

Foreign creditors have benefited enormously from the dollar’s privileged position. They have financed massive U.S. trade deficits that destroyed American industries while they pursued neo-mercantilist strategies. Many accumulated these Treasury securities not purely as market investments but as geopolitical tools or recycling mechanisms for their own export-led growth models. Their gains came at the direct expense of U.S. manufacturing employment and working-class wages. A selective default simply reverses a portion of that unfair transfer. It asserts the elementary nationalist principle that the credit of the American people exists to serve Americans first.

Critics will warn of catastrophic loss of trust, skyrocketing future borrowing costs, and the end of the dollar’s reserve status. These concerns are overstated. The United States possesses the world’s largest economy, unmatched military power, deep and liquid capital markets, and the simple reality that there are no perfect substitutes for the dollar in global trade and reserves. A selective default targeting only foreign official and large institutional holdings could be executed through legislation, regulatory action, or negotiated restructuring framed explicitly as a national emergency measure. Markets would adjust. Borrowing costs for the U.S. would likely rise modestly for a period, but the reduction in the real debt burden and the gains from improved trade balances and domestic investment would more than compensate. Nations that have restructured debt have often returned to markets faster than expected when underlying economic fundamentals were strong. America’s fundamentals remain the strongest in the world.

This strategy is nationalist because it places the concrete interests of American citizens—jobs, lower effective taxes, preserved entitlement programs, and reduced debt slavery—above abstract commitments to “global financial stability” that always seem to benefit creditors over debtors, foreigners over Americans. It rejects the post-1945 orthodoxy that America must act as the indispensable financial backstop for the world even as that role undermines its own industrial base and fiscal health.

The alternative is national decline through slow suffocation: ever-rising debt, increasing dependence on foreign capital, continued deindustrialization, and eventual politically imposed austerity that will fall hardest on the middle and working classes. A deliberate policy of devaluation and selective foreign default is the responsible choice of a sovereign nation that refuses to commit financial suicide out of misplaced deference to international norms written by creditors.

America should not stumble into default through crisis. It should choose this path deliberately, with eyes open, as a declaration of economic independence. The federal government’s first loyalty is to the American people. Currency devaluation and selective default on foreign debt are not radical departures from reality—they are the overdue correction of decades of elite delusion. It is time to put America first in American economic policy. The republic’s survival and prosperity depend on it.

The Case for Strategic Currency Devaluation and Sovereign Debt Restructuring: A Nationalist Economic Reckoning

Introduction

For decades, the United States has operated under a set of economic orthodoxies that treat currency stability, debt fidelity, and free capital flows as sacrosanct pillars of the international economic order. Yet the cumulative weight of trade deficits, mounting sovereign obligations, persistent deindustrialization, and the asymmetric distribution of globalization's costs demands a fundamental reexamination of these assumptions. This essay argues that a deliberate program of currency devaluation, coupled with selective sovereign debt default toward foreign creditors, represents not economic recklessness but a rational and justified nationalist strategy to rebalance the American economy, restore domestic productive capacity, and reclaim sovereign economic agency.

I. The Myth of Reserve Currency Invincibility

The United States occupies a unique position in the global economy as the issuer of the world's primary reserve currency. This "exorbitant privilege," as former French President Charles de Gaulle termed it, has long been celebrated as a source of national strength. However, a closer inspection reveals that this privilege has metastasized into a structural trap.

Because foreign nations require dollars for international trade, the United States has been able to consume far beyond its productive capacity, financing chronic current account deficits through foreign borrowing denominated in its own currency. The result has been the hollowing out of American manufacturing, the erosion of the industrial working class, and the accumulation of enormous external obligations. The reserve currency status has not been a blessing but a narcotic—providing short-term consumption gains while systematically undermining long-term productive competitiveness.

A deliberate devaluation would be the first step in breaking free from this trap. By reducing the purchasing power of the dollar on international markets, the United States would immediately improve the price competitiveness of domestic goods and services. Exports would surge, import substitution would accelerate, and the enormous trade deficits that have transferred trillions of dollars of purchasing power overseas would begin to correct. The argument that the United States must perpetually maintain a strong dollar serves the interests of financial elites and foreign creditors far more than it serves the American worker.

II. The Moral Economics of Sovereign Default

The sanctity of sovereign debt is perhaps the most fetishized principle in international finance. Every introductory economics textbook insists that sovereign default is catastrophic, irresponsible, and unthinkable. Yet this moral conviction conveniently overlooks the structural inequities embedded in the global debt system and the historical reality that sovereign default has been a recurring and often economically rational feature of statecraft.

Consider the asymmetry of the arrangement. Foreign creditors—whether sovereign wealth funds, central banks, or private institutional investors—hold trillions of dollars in U.S. Treasury securities. These purchases have been driven not by altruism but by profit-seeking and, in many cases, by the structural imperative to recycle dollar surpluses back into dollar-denominated assets. Creditors have earned substantial returns, often underwritten by implicit and explicit U.S. government guarantees. The relationship has been symbiotic only in the shallowest sense: foreign creditors have enjoyed risk-free carry trades while the United States has accumulated obligations that approach $35 trillion.

Selective default on sovereign debt owed to foreign creditors is a legitimate tool of economic statecraft. By restructuring or partially defaulting on debt held by foreign governments and institutions—particularly those of strategic competitors—the United States would accomplish several objectives simultaneously:

  1. Wealth repatriation: The fiscal space created by reduced debt servicing obligations could be redirected toward domestic infrastructure, healthcare, education, and industrial policy.
  2. Strategic leverage: Selective default against adversarial creditor nations would impose asymmetric costs, disrupting their sovereign wealth fund returns and dollar-denominated reserves.
  3. Domestic investment: Resources currently sent abroad as debt service payments would be retained within the domestic economy, generating multiplier effects that benefit American citizens directly.

III. Precedent and the Lessons of History

The assertion that currency devaluation and sovereign default represent economic heresy is historically illiterate. Throughout history, these instruments have been employed by serious nations pursuing serious economic objectives.

The United States itself defaulted on its debt obligations through the gold standard policies of the 1930s, when President Franklin Roosevelt devalued the dollar against gold by nearly 70% through Executive Order 6102 and the Gold Reserve Act of 1934. This deliberate devaluation was widely credited with stimulating recovery during the Great Depression by raising commodity prices, increasing the money supply, and boosting export competitiveness. No comparable economic catastrophe followed; instead, the American economy experienced its most sustained period of industrial growth in the ensuing decades.

More broadly, the history of sovereign default is replete with examples of nations that experienced robust recoverations following restructurings: Russia in 1998, Argentina multiple times through the 2000s, Iceland in 2008, and even the United Kingdom's deep restructuring after World War II. In each case, the feared contagion effects were temporary, while the long-term benefits of restoring economic sovereignty and correcting unsustainable obligations proved substantial.

Furthermore, the United States occupies a uniquely insulated position. Because the dollar is the global reserve currency, any devaluation directly reduces the value of foreign reserve holdings, effectively imposing a tax on nations that have accumulated dollar assets. This is not a weakness—it is leverage. No other nation possesses the structural power to implement such a policy with anything approaching the same asymmetric benefits.

IV. The Case of Devaluation as Industrial Policy

Perhaps the most compelling argument for deliberate currency devaluation is its relationship to industrial policy—a concept that has returned to the forefront of economic thinking. The United States has spent forty years pursuing free trade orthodoxies that have devastated its manufacturing base. Entire industries—steel, electronics, textiles, semiconductors—have migrated to low-cost jurisdictions, leaving behind hollowed communities and millions of displaced workers.

A weaker dollar would function as a comprehensive industrial policy without the need for cumbersome sector-specific subsidies or tariffs that invite retaliation. By making imports more expensive and exports more competitive, devaluation would shift relative prices in favor of domestic production. Supply chains that have been optimized for cost minimization at the expense of national resilience would be incentivized to reshore. The American worker, priced out by decades of offshoring and mass immigration, would find his labor relatively more competitive in a devaluated currency environment.

Critics will invoke the specter of inflation, and it is true that devaluation raises the cost of imported goods. But this objection reveals a fundamental misalignment of priorities. Moderate, controlled inflation—preferably directed against asset prices and imported luxury goods—is preferable to the slow-motion economic destruction wrought by deindustrialization, wage stagnation, and dependency on foreign supply chains. The inflation experienced by importing foreign goods is a transfer of wealth to foreign producers; domestically generated inflation, managed by monetary policy, represents a transfer of resources toward domestic economic activity. The choice between these two outcomes is the essence of nationalist economic reasoning.

V. Addressing the Foreign Creditor Moral Hazard

At its core, the argument for currency devaluation and selective default rests on a fundamental question of sovereignty and national priority. The postwar liberal international order was built on the assumption that cooperation, openness, and shared sacrifice would produce mutual benefit. A nationalist economic strategy that embraces deliberate devaluation and selective default is not reckless; it is long overdue. Currency devaluation—lowering the value of the dollar relative to other currencies—is a time-tested tool to enhance export competitiveness. Sovereign Primacy: The Case for Strategic Currency Devaluation and Selective Default

Introduction

The United States finds itself shackled by a financial architecture of its own creation—one that increasingly serves foreign creditors and international capital at the expense of American workers, communities, and long-term prosperity. While conventional economic orthodoxy treats sovereign debt obligations as sacrosanct and currency stability as an unqualified good, a clear-eyed assessment of national interest suggests otherwise. This essay argues that deliberate currency devaluation and selective default on foreign-held sovereign debt represent not reckless populism, but rational instruments of statecraft that the United States should deploy to reassert economic sovereignty, revitalize domestic industry, and rectify structural imbalances that have hollowed out the American middle class.

The Illusion of Unconditional Obligation

The premise that sovereign debt obligations are morally and practically absolute collapses under historical and philosophical scrutiny. Sovereign debt is not analogous to personal debt; nations do not choose their circumstances of birth, and the American people of today did not individually consent to obligations accumulated across decades of decisions made by rotating political administrations often captured by special interests.

More fundamentally, the social contract between a government and its citizens necessarily takes precedence over contracts with foreign creditors. When Thomas Jefferson wrote that "the earth belongs to the living," he articulated a principle with profound implications for intergenerational debt obligations. No generation possesses the moral authority to permanently bind its successors to financial arrangements that compromise their freedom and prosperity. The $34 trillion national debt—a substantial portion held by foreign governments and investors—represents precisely such an encumbrance.

The international financial system treats American debt obligations as inviolable while simultaneously tolerating, even facilitating, the mercantile practices of creditor nations that accumulated these holdings. China's currency manipulation, export subsidies, and intellectual property theft; Japan's decades of intervention to suppress the yen; Germany's exploitation of an artificially weak euro within a captive European market—these practices transferred trillions in wealth from American workers to foreign interests. The debt these nations now hold represents, in significant measure, the accumulated proceeds of economic warfare. Honoring it unconditionally means rewarding predation.

The Case for Strategic Devaluation

A deliberately weaker dollar would deliver immediate and substantial benefits to the productive economy. Manufacturing, agriculture, and tradeable services would gain competitive advantage overnight. The economic literature is unambiguous: currency depreciation shifts demand toward domestically produced goods and stimulates employment in trade-exposed sectors.

Critics will invoke inflation, but this concern requires contextualization. The United States has absorbed decades of deflationary pressure from cheap imports—a "benefit" whose costs were borne disproportionately by industrial workers in Michigan, Ohio, and Pennsylvania while coastal consumers enjoyed marginally cheaper goods. Moderate inflation that accompanies rebalancing represents a redistribution from asset holders and importers toward workers and producers. This is a feature, not a bug.

Furthermore, the current strength of the dollar reflects not economic fundamentals but the currency's role as global reserve. This "exorbitant privilege" is in fact an exorbitant burden—it structurally overvalues American labor in global markets, making domestic production uncompetitive regardless of worker productivity or skill. Economist Michael Pettis has documented how reserve currency status forces the United States to run persistent current account deficits, effectively exporting demand and jobs to maintain global liquidity. Strategic devaluation begins to unwind this trap.

The mechanism is straightforward: aggressive monetary expansion, explicit Federal Reserve commitment to a weaker dollar, and if necessary, direct intervention in currency markets. The United States has refrained from such measures out of ideological commitment to free markets and deference to trading partners, but this restraint is not reciprocated. Unilateral disarmament in currency competition has not produced multilateral cooperation; it has produced American deindustrialization.

Selective Default as Rational Policy

Selective default—prioritizing obligations to domestic holders while restructuring or repudiating debt held by foreign governments and their instrumentalities—represents the logical extension of national interest primacy. The distinction between domestic and foreign creditors is not arbitrary; it reflects fundamentally different relationships and interests.

American citizens and institutions holding Treasury securities are constituents whose interests the government exists to serve. Foreign governments holding American debt are strategic actors pursuing their own national interests, which frequently conflict with American prosperity. China's Treasury holdings are not passive investments; they are instruments of geopolitical leverage accumulated through systematic trade practices designed to disadvantage American workers.

The practical mechanics would involve legislation distinguishing sovereign creditor classes, with mandatory restructuring for foreign government holdings. Private foreign holders might receive differential treatment based on their home country's trade practices and reciprocal treatment of American investments. This targeted approach minimizes disruption to domestic financial markets while maximizing relief from the external debt burden.

Historical precedent supports the viability of this approach. Argentina's 2001 default and subsequent selective restructuring, while chaotic, ultimately produced a decade of rapid growth. Russia's 1998 default led to sustained economic expansion. Ecuador has defaulted multiple times without permanent exclusion from capital markets. Iceland's post-2008 decision to let foreign creditors of failed banks absorb losses—rather than socializing them onto citizens—produced faster recovery than countries that protected creditor interests by imposing austerity.

The United States, moreover, possesses advantages no other defaulting nation has enjoyed. The dollar's centrality to global trade, the depth of American capital markets, the military and political power of the American state—these assets virtually guarantee continued access to financing on terms the United States can dictate. Foreign creditors would face a choice between accepting restructured terms or holding worthless paper. The United States is not Greece, unable to print its own currency and subject to troika diktats. It is the issuer of the global reserve currency, and that position confers leverage that should be exercised.

Addressing the Orthodoxy's Objections

Conventional economists will offer several objections, each of which dissolves upon examination.

"Default would spike interest rates and borrowing costs." This prediction assumes creditors have alternatives offering equivalent safety and liquidity. They do not. Despite occasional threats, no substitute for Treasury securities exists as a store of value for global capital. Rising rates would primarily affect new borrowing, which disciplined fiscal policy should reduce regardless. Moreover, reduced debt service costs from restructuring would offset any increase in rates.

"Devaluation would impoverish Americans by raising import prices." This frames consumption as the purpose of economic life—a premise Americans increasingly reject. An economy exists to provide meaningful employment, community stability, and productive capacity, not simply to maximize consumer access to cheap foreign goods. The American worker who gains a manufacturing job cares little that imported electronics cost 15% more. Furthermore, import substitution effects would dampen inflationary impact over time as domestic production expands.

"International retaliation would devastate American exports." Retaliation how? America's trading partners already maintain undervalued currencies, export subsidies, and market barriers. The United States runs persistent trade deficits precisely because the playing field is already tilted against it. Retaliation from a position of mutual vulnerability differs from retaliation against an adversary that has been absorbing attacks without response.

"The rules-based international order would collapse." The "rules-based order" is a polite fiction that describes a system where the United States bears costs while others free-ride. When rules consistently produce outcomes contrary to American interests, the rules require revision. Other nations routinely default, devalue, and pursue mercantilist policies without triggering systemic collapse.

The Political Economy of Change

The greatest obstacle to these policies is not their economic impracticality but the political power of interests served by the status quo. Wall Street profits from the current dollar's role in global finance. Multinational corporations benefit from supply chains predicated on current exchange rates. Coastal elites whose consumption patterns depend on cheap imports resist policies making foreign goods more expensive.

These interests have captured both political parties, cloaking their preferences in the language of economic science. The bipartisan consensus around "free trade" and "sound money" represents not objective economic truth but the ideology of a class whose prosperity diverges from the nation's.

Breaking this consensus requires political leadership willing to articulate a different vision: an economy oriented toward production rather than consumption, toward employment rather than efficiency, toward national resilience rather than global integration. Devaluation and selective default are instruments of this reorientation, practical expressions of a philosophical commitment to economic nationalism.

The historical moment favors such leadership. Decades of globalization have produced stagnant wages, deindustrialization, regional depression, and social fragmentation documented by scholars from Charles Murray to Angus Deaton. The political manifestations—from Trump's tariffs to Sanders' anti-trade rhetoric—reveal widespread rejection of the neoliberal consensus. What remains is to translate this rejection into coherent policy.

A Program for Implementation

A serious program for currency devaluation and selective default would proceed as follows:

First, clear political authorization through legislative action establishing that the national interest takes precedence over international financial obligations, distinguishing creditor classes, and directing relevant agencies to pursue specified objectives.

Second, coordinated monetary action including Federal Reserve commitment to inflation targets above current levels, aggressive asset purchases expanding the monetary base, and explicit statements that dollar strength is contrary to policy objectives.

Third, executive measures including Treasury Department intervention in currency markets, restrictions on foreign government purchases of American debt, and renegotiation of debt held by foreign sovereigns under threat of legislative repudiation.

Fourth, complementary trade measures including tariffs calibrated to offset competitive devaluations by trading partners, preferential treatment for countries accepting restructuring terms, and domestic content requirements ensuring devaluation benefits translate into American employment.

Fifth, domestic stabilization including targeted support for citizens on fixed incomes most affected by inflation, incentives for domestic investment in productive capacity, and retraining programs for workers in import-competing sectors that will not revive.

This program would face fierce opposition from entrenched interests and face genuine short-term costs. But the alternative—continuing decline of productive America while financialized elites prosper—is no longer politically sustainable.

Conclusion

The argument advanced here will strike many readers as radical, even irresponsible. But the truly radical position is defending an international economic architecture that has produced forty years of wage stagnation, deindustrialization, and financial fragility while enriching a narrow cosmopolitan class. The truly irresponsible approach is continuing policies that predictably impoverish American communities while genuflecting before economic orthodoxies that serve foreign and elite interests.

Deliberately devaluing the currency and selectively defaulting on foreign-held debt represent not destabilizing adventurism but rational pursuit of national interest. Every serious nation prioritizes its citizens' prosperity over foreign creditors' claims. The United States, for too long, has been the exception. It is time to become a normal nation—a nation that uses the instruments of economic sovereignty to advance the interests of its own people.

The republic's founders rejected rule by distant powers indifferent to American welfare. That independence must now be reasserted in the economic domain. Currency and debt are tools of statecraft, not sacred obligations to be honored regardless of cost. Used strategically, they can begin the work of rebuilding an economy that serves all Americans rather than global capital and its domestic allies.

Standard economic analysis would contest many of these claims, particularly regarding default costs, inflation impacts, and market responses. Readers should consider counterarguments from conventional economics, international relations, and financial analysis.

Introduction

The Nixon shock of 1971 unilaterally abandoned the Bretton Woods gold convertibility commitment, effectively defaulting on international dollar obligations that foreign governments had been promised. These decisions are now taught as examples of pragmatic leadership rather than moral failure.

If Roosevelt and Nixon could execute what were functionally defaults and radical monetary restructuring when national circumstances demanded it, the taboo around these instruments is revealed as politically constructed rather than economically necessary. The question is not whether America has the capacity and precedent for such measures, but whether current circumstances justify them.

The Asymmetric Exploitation Argument

China holds approximately $800 billion in U.S. Treasury securities. Japan holds over $1 trillion. These holdings are not acts of generosity. They represent deliberate currency manipulation strategies by foreign governments that suppressed their own currencies for decades to capture American manufacturing jobs, hollow out industrial communities, and build export surpluses at American workers' expense.

The argument is straightforward: China and Japan accumulated these Treasury holdings as instruments of mercantilist economic warfare. They manipulated exchange rates, subsidized state enterprises, and engaged in systematic intellectual property theft while American factory towns collapsed. The Treasury holdings they accumulated represent, in economic substance, the profits of that strategy.

A selective default targeted at nations that have engaged in persistent currency manipulation and trade predation is not simply debt repudiation — it is a form of reparations accounting. The United States would be offsetting financial obligations against the economic damage inflicted by decades of mercantilist policy. American workers in Ohio and Pennsylvania who lost manufacturing careers to these policies received no compensation. Refusing to pay sovereign creditors who built their positions through economic aggression is arguably a more proportionate response than anything Washington has attempted through WTO complaints and tariff negotiations.

The "exorbitant privilege" of dollar reserve currency status comes with what economist Michael Pettis and others have described as an equally exorbitant burden. Because the world demands dollars as reserve assets, the United States is structurally compelled to run current account deficits. Foreign demand for dollar assets forces dollar appreciation, making American exports uncompetitive. The reserve currency role has systematically deindustrialized America not through American policy failures but through the structural mechanics of the international monetary system.

Deliberate dollar devaluation would rebalance this equation. A sustained 20-30% depreciation against major trading partners would:

  • Restore competitiveness to American manufacturing
  • Reduce the real burden of domestic debt obligations
  • Incentivize reshoring of industrial capacity

Sovereign default is a recognized instrument of international finance — Argentina, Greece, Russia, and dozens of other nations have employed it. The stigma attached to American default is partly a product of creditor-class ideology that benefits from treating debt repayment as a moral absolute.

A selective default that prioritized domestic investment — infrastructure, industrial policy, education, healthcare — over payments to foreign sovereign creditors would represent a legitimate democratic choice to prioritize citizens over bondholders. American citizens did not sign these loan agreements. Their elected representatives did, often in circumstances of dubious necessity.

Foreign holdings of U.S. debt represent a form of leverage that adversarial and competitive powers can theoretically exercise. The threat of coordinated Treasury selling — whether realistic or not — constrains American foreign policy. Decision-makers must consider how aggressive action against China, for instance, might interact with Chinese Treasury holdings. This is a structural vulnerability in American sovereignty.

Deliberately restructuring the debt profile to eliminate or reduce foreign sovereign holdings — even at the cost of a forced default — would enhance American strategic autonomy. A nation that does not owe significant financial obligations to geopolitical competitors operates with greater freedom of action. The short-term financial costs of default must be weighed against the long-term strategic benefit of sovereignty unencumbered by foreign creditor leverage.

The nationalist economic case for currency devaluation and selective sovereign default rests on interconnected arguments: historical precedent, asymmetric exploitation by mercantilist creditors, the industrial costs of reserve currency status, democratic legitimacy questions about debt accumulation, and strategic sovereignty considerations. The contagion problem is severe. A U.S. default would not primarily harm foreign governments — it would devastate money market funds, pension funds, insurance companies, and financial institutions globally and domestically that hold Treasuries as foundational "risk-free" assets. The 2008 crisis demonstrated how financial interconnection transmits shocks unpredictably.

Dollar devaluation has domestic victims. Inflation from currency devaluation is a regressive tax that disproportionately harms lower-income Americans with less capacity to hold inflation-hedging assets. The workers the nationalist argument purports to help would face higher prices for goods, energy, and imported inputs.

American consumers benefited from cheap goods; American companies profited from Chinese manufacturing; and the causal relationship between currency manipulation and manufacturing job losses competes with automation as an explanation.

Legal and institutional consequences would be substantial. Selective default based on nationality would likely violate treaty obligations and could trigger retaliatory expropriation of American assets abroad.

This essay should be understood as an exercise in argument construction, not a policy recommendation. The strongest version of an argument is not necessarily correct, and policies with these potential consequences warrant extreme scrutiny rather than adoption.

A Nationalist Case for Dollar Devaluation and Selective Sovereign Default

For decades, the United States has played the role of the world’s banker, bearing the costs and constraints of maintaining a “strong dollar” to appease foreign creditors and uphold the global financial order. I. Reclaiming Monetary Sovereignty Through Devaluation

The persistent overvaluation of the U.S. dollar has hollowed out domestic manufacturing, encouraged the outsourcing of jobs, and sustained an unhealthy reliance on cheap imports at the expense of homegrown production. A deliberate devaluation—executed in a controlled and strategic manner—would make American exports more competitive, reduce trade deficits, and stimulate the revival of domestic industries.

The reflexive moral outrage often directed at the idea of default is grounded less in economic reality than in the vested interests of foreign bondholders and financial elites. Sovereign default—especially when carefully targeted at obligations to external creditors—is not unprecedented, and it does not necessarily precipitate economic collapse. Argentina, Russia, and even the United States in 1933 and 1971 have altered or repudiated obligations when national interest demanded it.

Today’s U.S. public debt exceeds $34 trillion, and a significant portion is held by foreign governments, including geopolitical rivals such as China. Continuing to service these debts in full, at face value, effectively transfers American wealth abroad while constraining our ability to invest in infrastructure, education, and technological advancement at home. A selective default—focused on obligations held by non-allied foreign entities—would instantly relieve fiscal pressure and retain resources for domestic priorities. It is better to endure short-term capital market disruption than to mortgage the long-term prosperity and sovereignty of the republic.

III. Reducing Strategic Vulnerability

Foreign ownership of U.S. debt is more than an accounting matter—it is a strategic vulnerability. By holding vast amounts of Treasury securities, adversarial governments gain leverage over U.S. monetary policy. In any geopolitical crisis, they could dump these holdings, destabilizing markets and impairing U.S. economic strength. A policy of selective repudiation consolidates financial independence and signals that the nation will not allow its fiscal stability to be hostage to external powers.

Moreover, the adoption of devaluation and partial default as tools of policy would force a rebalancing of global trade patterns. Instead of foreign capital inflows funding unsustainable consumption, America would be incentivized to reinvest in domestic productivity, energy independence, and supply chain security.

IV. A Moral Imperative to Serve American Citizens First

The ultimate purpose of economic policy is not to preserve the balance sheets of foreign creditors but to advance the well-being of a nation’s citizens. Every dollar of interest paid to Beijing or Riyadh is a dollar not spent on American veterans, teachers, or entrepreneurs. Inflationary pressure from devaluation can be tempered by targeted subsidies for essential goods and aggressive domestic investment in supply-side capacity. Higher interest rates on future borrowing can be mitigated by financing through domestic savings programs and internal capital mobilization. Regarding reputation—global respect stems from power and self-reliance, not from servile adherence to a debt regime that undermines national prosperity.

Conclusion

The United States has the unique privilege—and responsibility—of controlling the world’s most critical currency and the world’s largest consumer market. This position should be used to secure prosperity for Americans first, not to underwrite the solvency and comfort of foreign bondholders. Deliberately devaluing the dollar and selectively defaulting on sovereign debt owed to rival nations is not a reckless abandonment of responsibility, but a calculated reassertion of sovereignty. It is the exercise of a nation’s right to place the welfare of its people above the conventions of a global financial order that has long demanded American sacrifice while delivering diminishing returns. Now is the time to reverse the flow—to ensure that America’s wealth stays in America.
